methods.label: Use the exterior tangent-angle bisectors
methods.explanation:
The figure shows the circle touching \(AB\) at \(S\), with \(R\) and \(T\) on the extensions of \(PB\) and \(PA\). Thus the angles between the tangent rays at \(A\) and \(B\) are exterior angles of triangle \(PAB\).

Let \(\alpha=\angle PAB\) and \(\beta=\angle PBA\). Since \(\angle APB=40^\circ\),
\[
\alpha+\beta=180^\circ-40^\circ=140^\circ.
\]
For two tangents drawn from an external point, the segment joining that point to the circle's center bisects the angle between the tangent rays. At \(A\), these rays are \(AB\) and \(AT\). Because \(AP\) and \(AT\) are opposite rays,
\[
\angle BAO=\frac{180^\circ-\alpha}{2}.
\]
At \(B\), the tangent rays are \(BA\) and \(BR\), while \(BP\) and \(BR\) are opposite rays. Therefore
\[
\angle ABO=\frac{180^\circ-\beta}{2}.
\]
Applying the angle sum in triangle \(AOB\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\angle AOB
&=180^\circ-\frac{180^\circ-\alpha}{2}
-\frac{180^\circ-\beta}{2}\\
&=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}=70^\circ.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{70^\circ}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
